vignette:
Amina was 35, an African American woman living with her partner and working as a tutor, when she first described the night that had split her life into “before” and “after.” She had been walking home from a late session, still carrying the day’s lesson plans, when she was raped. In the months that followed, she found that the assault had become fixed in her mind in a way that felt both vivid and strangely unreal. When she tried to speak about it, the words seemed to fail her; she would stop mid-sentence, look down, and say that she could not seem to put the frightening event into words, as though the experience belonged to someone else rather than to her. Yet when the memory surfaced, it did not feel distant or softened by time. It arrived with the same terror she had felt in the moment itself, and she would go pale, tense, and need to sit down until the feeling passed.

Amina was careful about who heard any part of her story. If friends or family brought up the attack, or even referenced it indirectly, she would become quiet and change the subject, uncomfortable with being reminded of it by others. She had come to dread not only discussion of the rape itself but also any situation in which she felt cornered by uncertainty. Unclear plans, unanswered messages, or situations where she did not know what would happen next made her feel on edge in a way she struggled to explain. What frightened her most was the sense that she could not prepare herself if something was about to go wrong. She spoke about uncertainty as if it were a physical threat, something that made her body tighten and her mind race ahead to worst-case outcomes.

Over time, Amina also noticed that nausea had become one of the clearest signs that she was being pulled back toward the event. At unexpected moments—sometimes while she was on her way to work, sometimes while she was waiting for her students to arrive—she would feel suddenly sick to her stomach. The sensation was especially unsettling because it seemed to come before any clear thought; her body would react first, and then she would realize she was frightened. In those moments she would want to get away, find water, and sit somewhere quiet until the feeling eased.

Her work as a tutor made some of these moments difficult to hide. She often worked with children in a small community setting, and the sound of kids crying could hit her with particular force. If a child in the next room began to cry, Amina would stiffen and lose her train of thought, her attention pulled away from the student in front of her. She would force herself to continue, but afterward she described feeling shaken and distracted, as if a familiar alarm had been set off inside her. Because she feared being unexpectedly reminded of the assault, she began arranging her sessions and errands to reduce contact with people who might ask personal questions or casually mention the attack. She avoided conversations that seemed likely to touch on that part of her life, and she became noticeably less open with colleagues and friends who had once been a source of comfort.

As weeks turned into months, Amina also started steering clear of anything that might make her feel happy or hopeful. She said it felt safer not to “get attached” to good moments, because hope made her feel vulnerable. Invitations, small celebrations, and plans that might have lifted her mood were often declined. Even when her partner tried to encourage her, she held back from enjoying herself too much, as if positive moments carried the risk of being taken away or proving that she had misjudged how damaged she really was. She had come to believe that she had permanently changed for the worse. In her more difficult moments, she told herself that she was not the same woman she had been before the rape, and that something in her had been altered in a way that could not be undone. She also believed that if she thought about the event directly, she would not be able to handle it, so she tried to push it away whenever it surfaced. That effort did not erase the memory; it only made each accidental reminder feel more sharp and alarming.

By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by the effort of holding herself together. Her relationship had become narrower, with fewer easy conversations and less shared planning. She remained committed to her partner and her work, but she was tired of managing the same waves of terror, nausea, and self-blame on her own. She described repeatedly blaming herself for what happened, turning the assault over in her mind even when she knew it left her feeling worse. What finally brought her in was the fear that she could not keep living as if she had to brace for impact all the time. She wanted relief from the terror that still rose when the memory came back, and she hoped, cautiously, that she might find a way to face it without feeling that she would fall apart.
